correctness.rationale: The backward equations give oriented endpoint hitting times as the sums of cumulative stationary masses and complementary masses divided by conductances. Every other oriented hitting time is a positive subinterval sum. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz yields the exact scalar dual lower bound, and strictly concave scalar maximization selects an allocation that attains it. Endpoint derivative signs determine the worst direction; strict convexity yields a unique global conductance vector. The explicit right-of-center surcharge threshold follows from the derivative at the boundary. A controlled integrable-singularity Riemann sum gives the two distinct quadratic and quartic price-scaling laws. The bundled program passed 19,538 supplementary finite checks, including direct hitting-equation solves and numerical competing allocations; finite checks are not used as proof of the infinite claims.

broader_coverage.reasoning: Convex resistance optimization supplies a methodological predecessor but no theorem dominating this asymmetric first-passage objective with external stationary masses. For three vertices with prices \((1,3)\), max-resistance minimization yields conductance ratio \(\sqrt{3}\), whereas the robust mean-hitting minimizer yields \(\sqrt{3/2}\). Neither solution implies the other. General convexity alone does not provide the explicit threshold or its two scaling exponents. Berman 1964 provides a broad PERT convex-resource precedent, potentially encompassing general minimax reciprocal-cost design via reductions. Its abstract does not claim the fixed-stationary path one-defect threshold or position-sensitive quadratic/quartic law, but the full text was not accessible; this is an explicit priority risk rather than a whole-document negative claim.

value.rationale: The exact all-price, all-fixed-stationary-law classification solves the natural robust resource allocation problem minimizing the slowest ordered-state traversal on a reversible path. It is more than an elementary symmetric resistance allocation because price asymmetry changes which directional hitting constraint is active. The explicit exact surcharge boundary and its different quadratic versus quartic scaling when an expensive link moves toward the midpoint identify a meaningful large-system design crossover. The one-price family is motivated by the general model, not an arbitrary numerical slice. The result has no claim for general graphs or tail control.
